stories.summary: On London’s eastern fringe in Essex, data centre operator Nscale plans to build its £2 billion ($3.8 billion) flagship UK facility across the road from where the Bank of England produces bank notes.
stories.content:
On London’s eastern fringe in Essex, data centre operator Nscale plans to build its £2 billion ($3.8 billion) flagship UK facility across the road from where the Bank of England produces bank notes.

It’s a symbolic site. The heady rush for artificial intelligence had created a sense that data centres were a licence to print money for the likes of its owner, Josh Payne, a former Hunter Valley coal miner.

Power supplies to NextDC’s controversial M3 data centre expansion in Melbourne had been delayed, the developer said on Monday, as trading in its shares was halted pending an update on the potential hit to its balance sheet.

The company’s M3 data centre in West Footscray, used to process artificial intelligence services, is located just 15 metres away from some homes and has drawn complaints from local residents about noise levels, emissions and new electricity infrastructure.

stories.title: PM: Malaysia must plan data centre growth to attract quality investments
stories.summary: KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 19): Malaysia must strategically plan the growth of its data centre industry to attract quality investments, strengthen the digital economy and ensure the sustainable use of energy and water while protecting the environment, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 19): Malaysia must strategically plan the growth of its data centre industry to attract quality investments, strengthen the digital economy and ensure the sustainable use of energy and water while protecting the environment, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.

He said infrastructure readiness, energy supply and resource-use efficiency required closer scrutiny as the country sought to develop the industry sustainably.

Anwar said this in a post on X, after chairing the National Economic Action Council (MTEN) meeting on Monday.

The meeting also reviewed the Circular Economy Framework (RKEK), which aims to improve resource efficiency, reduce waste and promote the reuse of products and materials for as long as possible before they become waste.

“Effective coordination across sectors, ministries and agencies is needed to ensure the circular economy approach is implemented comprehensively and sustainably,” he said.

stories.title: Australia's NEXTDC halts share trading before update on data centre power delay
stories.summary: BENGALURU (Oct 19): Australia's NEXTDC on Monday said its shares had been placed on a trading halt pending a market update it will provide on the impact of a delay in power supply to its M3 Melbourne data centre.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
BENGALURU (Oct 19): Australia's NEXTDC on Monday said its shares had been placed on a trading halt pending a market update it will provide on the impact of a delay in power supply to its M3 Melbourne data centre.

The data centre operator said it expects to make an announcement within two days, adding that its board is yet to meet to assess the delay and its implications.

Analysts at Citi said that the delay likely relates to electricity distributor Jemena pausing work on electricity lines meant to deliver power to M3.

That would likely delay the billing from M3, which represents around 70 megawatts (MW) of the 155 MW of incremental billing in the state of Victoria the brokerage assumed for fiscal year 2027, it added.

NEXTDC said the trading halt would allow the company to meet its continuous disclosure obligations while it evaluates the impact of the power supply delay, including any potential effect on its fiscal 2027 financial guidance.

In August, the company forecast underlying earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for fiscal 2027 to be between A$385 million and A$410 million (US$268.27 million to US$285.69 million).

Citi said that while it is likely the whole billing capacity for M3 is not impacted, the delay could put at risk around A$25 million in NEXTDC's operating earnings for fiscal 2027.

stories.title: Microsoft withdraws from Nscale’s UK AI data center plans
stories.summary: Microsoft has withdrawn from the UK’s largest AI data center project in Loughton, Essex over concerns about electricity supplies. Nscale, a British vertically integrated, full-stack AI infrastructure and neocloud company remains committed to the facility’s development which was announced in 2025, and originally expected to be completed in 2027. The project was backed by the […]
stories.content:
Microsoft has withdrawn from the UK’s largest AI data center project in Loughton, Essex over concerns about electricity supplies. Nscale, a British vertically integrated, full-stack AI infrastructure and neocloud company remains committed to the facility’s development which was announced in 2025, and originally expected to be completed in 2027. The project was backed by the UK government as a major part of its plans to expand the UK’s artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Microsoft had been expected to fund a supercomputer at the site and act as its anchor customer. Its withdrawal leaves Nscale without an official public customer for the Essex facility. The setback follows reports that electricity supply problems would delay the project’s connection to the national grid as reported by the BBC.

“We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK,” Nscale told the BBC. “Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term. This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

Microsoft declined to comment on the partnership termination.

Nscale is also reportedly preparing for a potential New York stock market listing this year, with a possible valuation of £ 26 billion (US$ 35 billion). Delays to major projects and the loss of a significant customer could complicate those plans. Microsoft’s withdrawal could create further uncertainty around Nscale’s expansion plans and attract greater investor scrutiny ahead of its planned US initial public offer (IPO) on the New York stock market listing according to the Guardian.

The two companies continue to work together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States. The withdrawal raises questions about the project’s delivery and Nscale’s wider expansion plans, supported by Nvidia, is among the businesses selected to support the government’s ambition to establish domestic AI computing capacity.

The company is also exploring other expansion sites in the UK.Nscale filed for an initial public offering in the US last month. # Microsoft exits Nscale UK data centre deal over power delays

Microsoft has reportedly ended its agreement for Nscale's Loughton data centre in the UK. This decision comes amid repeated delays in securing a power supply for the facility.

- Published On Oct 19, 2026 at 07:30 AM IST

## Highlights

- Microsoft reportedly ended its data centre agreement with Nscale for the Loughton, UK facility.
- Power supply for the Loughton data centre is not expected until the 2030s, according to grid officials.
- Nscale stated its relationship with Microsoft remains strong, and other contracts are unaffected.
- Nscale is exploring alternative power sources for the UK site and other expansion opportunities.

stories.title: GreenSquare SYD1 opens first stage after adaptive reuse of 1995 data center
stories.summary: Australian data center operator GreenSquare today announced that the first stage of its SYD1 data centre campus in Norwest Business Park, Western Sydney, is now operational, following the adaptive reuse of a data center originally opened in 1995. The AI-ready data center was completed and ready for service in eight months with Australian neocloud Sharon AI […]
stories.content:
Australian data center operator GreenSquare today announced that the first stage of its SYD1 data centre campus in Norwest Business Park, Western Sydney, is now operational, following the adaptive reuse of a data center originally opened in 1995.

The AI-ready data center was completed and ready for service in eight months with Australian neocloud Sharon AI being its first customer. Sharon AI is deploying approximately 8,200 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs, a significant deployment of NVIDIA HGX B300 infrastructure in Australia.

GreenSquare retained the existing slab and much of the structure rather than demolishing and rebuilding. The data halls were relocated to the ground floor, to accommodate latest-generation, high-density compute without additional structural reinforcement. This increased IT capacity by 275 per cent while substantially reducing structural carbon.

SYD1 has a projected power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.20 and potable water usage effectiveness (WUE) of less than 0.1 litres per kilowatt-hour, both below the NSW Government guideline benchmarks of 1.25 and 1.0, respectively. It uses a closed-loop cooling system and rainwater harvesting.

An independent assessment by engineering consultants TTW found that the adaptive reuse retained 92 per cent of the building’s existing structural carbon. Combined with low-carbon concrete, it resulted in 76 per cent lower structural upfront carbon per square metre and 93 per cent lower carbon per kilowatt of IT capacity compared with a new-build facility.

Main construction works began in February 2026 with more than 350,000 hours of work recorded without a lost-time injury. About 400 people worked on site at peak time with teams operating around the clock during critical stages of the construction.

The NSW Government’s Investment Delivery Authority has endorsed a proposed 80 MW second stage. GreenSquare is backed by programs managed by Partners Group.

GreenSquare Chief Technology Officer, Joshua Martens, said: “We saw an opportunity to give a 30-year-old data centre a completely new purpose. By rethinking the building’s configuration, introducing prefabricated systems design, and using the latest technology to reduce carbon, we’ve created a facility that can support some of today’s most demanding compute requirements while using resources far more efficiently.”

stories.title: AI cloud firm Nscale faces investor pushback over IPO valuation
stories.summary: This comes after its investor Microsoft pulled out of a UK data centre deal with the firm
stories.content:
This comes after its investor Microsoft pulled out of a UK data centre deal with the firm

\[NEW YORK\] Nscale is facing opposition to the valuation target it is pursuing in its initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter, after a series of market setbacks for artificial intelligence companies.

The Nvidia-backed data centre developer has been seeking an IPO valuation of about US$30 billion, the people said.

A cohort of investors have lately urged that a valuation in the US$16 billion to US$19 billion range would be more likely to find favour with buyers, in light of factors including the implosion of Australian AI data centre company Firmus’ IPO plan, some of the people said.

A disconnect over valuation would add to recent challenges facing Nscale’s planned IPO.

Microsoft, an investor in the company as well as a client, pulled out of a UK data centre deal with Nscale, the company said on Sunday (Oct 18), after the site was contending with delays from power constraints.

Sentiment toward AI infrastructure companies including chipmakers and cloud computing firms has turned as borrowing costs have risen and uncertainty over the technology’s long-term payoff has grown.

A discrepancy in expectations between a company seeking an IPO and potential investors can pressure a firm to slow down the process.

The so-called valuation gap may reflect differing outlooks on where funding costs are likely to go and whether challenges to the broader sector may be quickly resolved.

Nscale filed publicly for a US listing on Sep 18, and has yet to begin formal marketing even though the required 15-day waiting period has elapsed.

The company is working through comments from the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on its filing, and intends to kick off marketing when those are resolved, people familiar with the matter said.

Deliberations are ongoing, details of the IPO plan could change and no final decisions have been made, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information is not public.

A representative for Nscale declined to comment.

The SEC did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal office hours.

The London-based firm raised US$3.36 billion in a pre-IPO financing round in September in a deal led by Dan Loeb’s Third Point with investors including Nvidia, Apollo Global Management, Citadel, Hudson Bay Capital and Abu Dhabi Investment Council participating.

Stock prices for several of Nscale’s peers have been battered.

CoreWeave wiped out a quarter of its market value last week as a measure of its credit risk climbed to an all-time high, and Nebius Group’s stock slumped 32 per cent in the past two weeks.

Nscale, which is developing data centres in locations including Norway and West Virginia, was expected to raise as much as US$3 billion in its IPO, Bloomberg News reported in August.

The Norway facility, just north of the Arctic Circle, is billed as a flagship site for the British data centre developer, but construction is six months behind schedule, set back by leaks in the cooling system, local regulations, construction delays and a fire, Bloomberg News reported.

Bankers have faced a cocktail of risks which is threatening to stall the IPO market for deals outside of Anthropic after smart-ring maker Oura and Bamboo Insurance Services were forced to postpone debuts as interest rates climbed higher and the Iran war dragged on.

The expectation that Anthropic could meet or exceed SpaceX’s record-setting debut as soon as November has also presented a hurdle for Wall Street. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: The end of independent infrastructure roadmaps: how AI is forcing data center co-design
stories.summary: Idle accelerators represent stranded capital, wasted energy, and lower returns on some of the most expensive infrastructure investments in the data center
stories.content:
For decades, most data center infrastructure evolved as a collection of largely independent technology domains. Processor performance improved through architectural and process innovations, memory and networking advanced on their own roadmaps, and facility infrastructure scaled predictably to support successive generations of hardware.

Moore's Law, standardized interfaces, and steady technology scaling allowed operators to upgrade servers, networks, and facilities on different timelines with confidence. AI has fundamentally changed that model. Today’s accelerator platforms derive their performance not from compute engines alone, but from the interaction of memory subsystems, networking fabrics, advanced packaging technologies, power delivery systems, and cooling infrastructure.

As AI deployments scale, the traditional separation between these domains is diminishing. What was historically viewed as a collection of independent infrastructure layers is now operating more as a tightly coupled system in which decisions made in one domain influence the outcomes across others.

Unlike traditional enterprise workloads, where performance improvements could often be realized within a single subsystem, large-scale AI training and inference are constrained by the efficiency with which data moves across the entire platform. Every training iteration requires continuous movement and synchronization of model parameters, activations, and gradients across thousands of accelerators, making memory capacity, memory bandwidth, interconnect latency, and communication overhead as critical to performance as the compute engines themselves.

Hence, idle accelerators represent stranded capital, wasted energy, and lower returns on some of the most expensive infrastructure investments in the data center.

## Evidence from recent AI infrastructure deployments

Recent AI infrastructure deployments illustrate these dependencies clearly. Modern accelerator platforms are increasingly designed around the integration of compute, memory, networking, power delivery, and cooling systems rather than advances in any single component.

The adoption of high-bandwidth memory has highlighted the growing importance of memory bandwidth and advanced packaging, while power availability and cooling capacity have emerged as major deployment constraints for large-scale AI clusters. Together, these developments demonstrate that system performance increasingly depends on co-design rather than independent optimization.

The clearest evidence of this shift is organizational as much as technical. Nvidia'sintegration of GPUs, NVLink, NVSwitch, networking, CUDA, and DGX systems, Google's co-design of TPUs with its software stack and data center infrastructure, and the emergence of vertically integrated platforms such as AWS Trainium and Microsoft's Maia all reflect the same underlying trend.

Competitive advantage now comes from minimizing inefficiencies across the entire compute system and optimizing interactions across hardware, software, networking, and infrastructure.

Architectural decisions can also no longer be evaluated in isolation. For instance, adding more accelerator compute delivers little value unless memory bandwidth scales alongside it.

Meeting those demands often requires additional HBM, advanced packaging, and higher power delivery, which in turn increases thermal density and drives the adoption of liquid cooling and high-density rack architectures. These denser systems also place greater demands on networking, requiring higher-bandwidth, lower-latency fabrics to keep thousands of accelerators synchronized efficiently.

Additionally, facility power and cooling constraints can limit achievable performance regardless of silicon capability. In AI infrastructure, every attempt to remove one bottleneck influences multiple others, making overall performance a function of how effectively the broader platform is optimized as a single system.

## **Implications for infrastructure and technology roadmaps**

Modern accelerator roadmaps now embed assumptions about the infrastructure in which they operate. Memory, packaging, networking, power delivery, and thermal management are no longer implementation details but architectural constraints.

Consequently, selecting an accelerator has become inseparable from evaluating whether the surrounding infrastructure can support it. An accelerator designed for multi-terabyte-per-second memory bandwidth and kilowatt-scale power consumption cannot achieve its intended performance in facilities built for previous generations of compute.

For operators, accelerator selection now extends beyond silicon performance to include the power, cooling, and connectivity required to support it.

The implications extend beyond technology selection to infrastructure planning itself. For colocation providers, facility roadmaps may increasingly be driven by customer accelerator deployments rather than traditional refresh cycles, requiring earlier investments in power distribution, liquid cooling, and high-density rack architectures.

For hyperscalers, the trend reinforces the need for tighter coordination across silicon, networking, software, and facility design. In both cases, decisions across silicon, networking, software, and facility engineering are becoming more interdependent, with infrastructure strategy and compute strategy evolving together.

## **Conclusion**

The AI compute stack is now defined by how effectively its components operate together. As supporting technologies become more tightly integrated with accelerator architectures, the traditional boundaries between infrastructure domains continue to blur.

For operators, infrastructure strategy and compute strategy are becoming inseparable, requiring decisions to be evaluated in the context of the broader system. As AI deployments continue to scale, competitive advantage will increasingly depend not on the performance of any individual component, but on how effectively the entire platform is co-designed and operated as a unified system.

*This article was written in collaboration with Vignesh Sathiyamoorthy, a technologist in Microsoft’s SCHIE (Silicon, Compute Hardware, Infrastructure Engineering) organization.*

In the article, the AI compute stack refers to the collection of technologies required to deliver large-scale AI training and inference workloads, including accelerators, memory, networking, power delivery, cooling systems, and the supporting datacenter infrastructure that enables them to operate as a unified platform.

stories.title: Microsoft scraps UK data centre deal with Nscale, Telegraph says
stories.summary: The facility’s site has been contending with a series of delays, the newspaper adds

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic
The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
The facility’s site has been contending with a series of delays, the newspaper adds

\[LONDON\] Microsoft has pulled out of a UK data centre deal with British neocloud Nscale at a critical time for the startup’s initial public offering hopes, the *Telegraph* reported.

The newspaper did not provide a specific reason for why the US tech giant had pulled the plug on the deal in Loughton, Essex, though it said the site has been contending with a series of delays.

Authorities have told Nscale they do not expect a power supply to the facility until the 2030s, it added.

Nscale’s flagship site in Norway is also six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts (MW) of the intended 30 MW data centre up and running.

Nscale relies on Microsoft and Anthropic for around 85 per cent of its contracts, going by an IPO filing, and the former had been set to become the anchor tenant at Nscale’s first British data centre in Essex.

Microsoft’s withdrawal would mark a setback for the company that is seeking to raise as much as US$3 billion in an IPO as soon as October, and which was already contending with investor jitters over the risks of the wider artificial intelligence build-out.

Nscale is one of the most prominent neoclouds, a new group of companies seeking to build huge computer complexes for AI.

They want to cash in on the hundreds of billions of dollars big tech companies have pledged to spend on the technology and are a key part of the AI boom’s supply chain.

An Nscale spokesperson told the *Telegraph*: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

Microsoft did not comment to the *Telegraph* and did not immediately respond to queries by Bloomberg.

The backdrop to Nscale’s IPO ambitions has turned gloomier in recent days, with fellow neocloud CoreWeave in the spotlight last week after the co-founder said the company was exploring ways to borrow in investment-grade debt markets, where there are vast pools of money from insurers to tap.

Investors had already grown cautious of AI computing suppliers due to the tens of billions of dollars they and their customers are borrowing to finance the massive build-out of data-centre capacity.

CoreWeave shares plunged in the first three sessions of the week, then bounced back somewhat, before concern returned on Friday, leading to the the stock’s worst week since November with a 25 per cent drop.

That also came in the wake of Australian data centre company Firmus scrapping its plans for an IPO, after the deal failed to garner enough support for the marketed share price. BLOOMBERG
